utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. All the accused are here. From the Prosecution teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek -- or from the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek, Mr. Haynes, and Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution team is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nice to see you again. We are doing our utmost to try and finish with your testimony without need for you to return. I don't know how successful we will be; but in the past, the Prosecution and Defence teams have been very cooperative. So let's keep our fingers crossed and give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off with you mentioning a Colonel Vukovic, in addition to Major Nikolic, as two VRS commanders with whom you had some meetings prior to July of 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you describe, roughly, how frequently you would meet with either one of those two men, and where you would meet them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll start with Major Nikolic, who we could meet as often as possible, in that if there was anything that we required to know or to check or to give information to the BSA side, this was our main contact. This is the guy we always communicated with through our interpreter, and this could be as often as maybe even twice a week, once a week, or something like that. For Colonel Vukovic, it was not that often. I think during my stay there, for meetings, we met about two or three times, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where would these meetings take place, for example, with Major Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Major Nikolic, we would normally meet at the point that we were calling "Yellow Bridge." This was a point somewhere in between Potocari and Bratunac. So that is where we would meet, and it was sort of a check-point for them. There were soldiers there. So they would come from the BSA side and we come from the Srebrenica side, and we meet there and discuss whatever we wanted to discuss. Also, it's worth noting that at times we would meet in a hotel, Hotel Fontana, inside Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would these contacts be initiated solely by yourself or your fellow UNMOs or would Major Nikolic read out to you through Petar as well on occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances, it would be Major Nikolic, himself, requesting to meet us, due to some issues that maybe he wanted us to discuss; and at other times, it could be ourselves initiating the discussion or even Dutch-Bat. Dutch-Bat could at times request for a meeting with us and Major Nikolic at the Yellow Bridge or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what types of matters would these meetings cover?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the times these issues that we were discussing would cover areas like the general condition of the enclave; the issues concerning the Muslims themselves; the BSA side; also issues concerning, especially when we are the ones that requested it or the Dutch-Bat, issues concerning the UNHCR convoys; or even during the time that our UNMOs had gone out and there was no replacement, requesting them to see whether they can allow new ones to come in so that they can replace the ones who have already gone. So there were various issues that we would discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Major Nikolic, or Colonel Vukovic, or any of the Serb military representatives with whom you met ever complain to you about the fact that Muslim forces were attacking, from inside the enclave, outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an occurrence that I really don't remember whether it ever happened, because most of the accusations on attacks were coming from the BiH, saying that they had been attacked by the BSA, but normally not the other way around, not the BSA complaining about attacks from the BiH. It was, I think, very rare or never occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that -- I take it that you are restricting this information or this answer that you've just given to the reports that you received, personally, or are you including also knowledge of other reports received by others, UNHCR, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mainly restricting myself to what we, as observers, got. If there was any report maybe from Dutch-Bat that maybe never came to our attention, I really do not know. But from the observer side, it's not necessarily me, but also including the other military observers that we had there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, whatever the reason for a particular meeting with the VRS representatives, was there anything in particular that they repeated to you during the course of those meetings that stands out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one thing that was very clear in their minds and in most of the discussions that we had is that they would like the Muslims to leave the enclave. The way in which they would leave the enclave varied from individual to individual, but mainly they had these as the main agenda, that they really want the Muslims to leave the enclave, so that it can be free of Muslims and it can be inhabited by the normal people who are Serbs. To them, they always claimed that that enclave belonged to the Serbs and that they could not have Muslims in their -- in their midst, so they just wanted the Muslims to leave that enclave. At one point, they even alluded to the fact that they would give the Muslims passage to get out, so that they leave the enclave to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was it your understanding, based on what they were telling you, that when you refer to "Muslims," was that referring to only the military of the Muslim population or the civilian and military population together leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when they said they wanted the Muslims out, to them it was not just the military element. It meant both the military and the civilian component. So they had no doubts in their minds, in their utterances, in their discussions, that they really wanted all the Muslims away from that enclave so that they can re-occupy the place as Serbs; because to them, it belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a conclusion that you arrived at at the time or is it a conclusion that you have arrived at after the events; and in any case, on what do you base it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is even written in one of -- I think partly in my statement that I gave and also in some of the sitreps that they said they wanted the Muslims to leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And perhaps I can follow up, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention to a dinner meeting you had at the Hotel Fontana in June of 1995, at which Colonel Vukovic was present. Do you recall that meeting, and if you do, would you just describe the events that occurred in that meeting for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a meeting that was called by Major Nikolic and his team, and they wanted us to meet in that hotel with some senior BSA officers. They did not tell us the agenda of the meeting. But when we arrived there, there were several senior officers, including Colonel Vukovic. And during the discussion that we had there, Colonel Vukovic was very clear in his own words, saying that, "We should tell -- go and tell the Muslims to pack up and leave Srebrenica. We do not want them there." Then he went on further to say that he could give them safe passage to get out of the enclave; and if not, if they do not want to get out on their own will, he's going to kill them. That was very clear, those were the instructions that he gave, those were his words. And to was, we took it like he was being very clear. He was telling them, actually, "You better leave; and if you don't want to leave willingly, we will clear the enclave of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in June of 1995, did anything happen that affected the size of your team?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the time that some of the UNMOs who were inside the enclave finished their times of staying there. In fact, if we start slightly before that, we had every month, after working 30 days, a UNMO would be given six days off so that he can go back to Zagreb or whatever he wants, so that he can relax, and come back already refreshed so that he can be used better. During that period, that is, somewhere after April, they started denying the UNMOs, that is, the BSA started denying the UNMOs permission to leave the enclave. So there was a long stay until three observers were due now for rotation, and the BSA said they cannot give clearance for them to get out. So, later on, they allowed them to get out; and upon their exit, they said they cannot allow anybody else to come in to replace them. So, in effect, we were left, just the three of us; me, myself; Major Andre De Haan from Holland; and Major David Tetteh from Ghana. Those were the only observers who were left in the enclave at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Thayer. Did you leave issue of the meeting at Hotel Fontana with Colonel Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thought I had, but I sense that we haven't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, out of the three UNMOs who you just described, was any of -- were any of you assigned to be the team leader?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Andre De Haan was the UNMO who was appointed as the team leader, and he started functioning the same way as the team leader. Until later on when he got sick and admitted, we were left there, just the two of us, me and David Tetteh.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to turn your attention now to the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave. Do you recall where you were when the attack commenced on 6 July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 6th of July, that is when the final assault on Srebrenica started, and we were sleeping in the PTT building when we heard shelling all over the place. That was around somewhere 3.00, around 3.00 or somewhere there, in the early hours of the morning. That is when we heard shells in large quantities, because shelling in Srebrenica sometimes was obviously not -- was actually a norm; but at that time, it was continuous shelling. So we realised something is going on. So we went to the bunker and listened, counted the shells, then came out, started sending reports, and we knew for sure there was something that was actually happening, something that looked like it's a serious business.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe the shelling that you're observing and hearing and counting during this first day of the attack on 6 July? Was there any pattern that you began to perceive?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pattern was almost definite. It was like they were shelling a few shells -- not a few, you know, you're talking 50 and over shells; then stop for a while; and, after a while, they would come back and shell again. They had formed a system whereby they were starting from the one side of the village, going upwards. So, in that, you know, we were also interpreting that way, because at least we wanted to know what is really happening. And when we caught that pattern, we realised there could be a safe period in between when we could get out of the bunkers, go and see what is really happening on ground -- on the ground itself, analyse the craters. Then maybe if they're sick, we take them to hospital, injured. For those killed, we count and report and all that. We found that to be almost a bit systematic. They had a system, a pattern that they had formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, by this time on July 6th, how many UNMOs do you recall being operational and were actually working in Srebrenica with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the UNMOs who were there were just the two of us, me and Major David Tetteh, just the two of us in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to bunkers. Where was your bunker located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our bunker, Your Honour, was located below the PTT building, and that is like an underground floor, you know. Below where we were, where we were living, under there was something that was sort of a bunker. That is where we were going to hide ourselves from the shelling, at least to feel that we were a bit safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you able to still count the detonations from inside that bunker, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there, we could, because the shells, you know, they make a loud bang, and you could count all of them. You can't count all of them. In the whole of Srebrenica itself, I mean the town itself, all the way up to Potocari, you would be able to count, because you could hear and the noise is accurate, definite. I mean, you can hear it from wherever you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described, Colonel, a safe period that you detected in this pattern of shelling. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you and Major Tetteh did during those safe periods and what you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, in the first place, this was a very trying moment for both of us. It's the first time we had such a serious situation in the whole AOR, that is, area of responsibility, and now we are left just the two of us. So flexibility got minimised a bit, in that with many you are able to send some out, some would go for patrols, some would do this and that, some would write reports, but now we are just the two of us. How do you do it? How do you go about the business of knowing what is happening outside? And we had a minimum number of observers who could go out; that is, two. So what do you do? We decided that in the absence of additional observers, we had to at least use ourselves and make sure that we get a proper count of what is happening in the enclave. So we decided that one of us would be going out with one of the interpreters. In one vehicle, go out and check what is happening; first of all, know how the shelling is, the effects of the shelling in the enclave; the injured, if there are any; the killed, if there are any; also analyse the craters as much as one could within as short a time as possible; then come back and start making the report. By that time, the other person now can also go out. If the pattern has started again, he can also go out, do the same, and we were rotating like that. So, in essence, what I'm saying is that we wanted to do everything within the shortest time possible and with a minimum number of people that we had; that is, just the two of us. So that is exactly what we did. But in the process, also we managed to inform the people, that is, the inhabitants of the town, that they should not get out. We tried to sensitize them, you know, with as much effort as we could, saying, "The pattern that is coming now, you people will be killed. So please stay off the streets, stay off everywhere else. Just go to your houses and stay there." Of course, it was difficult to achieve this, but at least we tried as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, based on your experience in Srebrenica, were you aware of whether or not people did have shelters, bunkers, or safe places to go?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, there were a few bunkers. In most of the houses, there was some safe areas under, but, of course, they could not be enough for the whole population of that place. So even if we were telling them to do that, most of them would still be in their own houses, normal areas of their dwelling, because there were not enough bunkers. But at least we informed them to try and be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, would you please describe the casualties, if any, that you personally observed during this first day of shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during this first day of shelling, the casualties, we had several- just a few, actually - who had shrapnel injuries, that is, to the head, some to the whole body, their legs, and all that; but, surprisingly, the number was not high. It was not high. I cannot remember how many, but there were a few. We took a few to hospital. Actually, it was surprisingly low. Despite the heavy shelling, the number of casualties were very low, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll talk about that in a few moments. Did you stay in Srebrenica, do you recall, that first day, or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that day, I think - I think - I just stayed in Srebrenica. I'm not very sure, but I think I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you manage to report the events of this first day to your UNMO sector headquarters in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did. In fact, every event, we were reporting to our headquarters as soon as it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 490 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you read it okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what this particular document is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, these are normal sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just explain the "from," "to," and "info" lines that appear towards the top of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From," here it shows that it's from UNMO headquarters sector BH, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina Northeast. That is the sector that we had. That was our own sector. And "To," this is to the UNMO headquarter BH Command. The "From" is actually from Tuzla, and the BH Command was in Sarajevo. Then "Info," MIO, that is a military information officer, UNMO headquarters, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one more definition, sir. At paragraph 2, there's an acronym there, "SMO," "SMO's assessment." What does "SMO" stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the senior military observer; that is, the one in charge of a sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So he or she would have been based, in this case, in Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 3, do you see the portion that begins: "Team Srebrenica reported a BSA offensive launched and ongoing."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference to at least 250 artillery and mortar rounds "have been recorded so far." Do you recall where that information as to the specific figure of 250 artillery and mortar rounds came from?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure, these -- these came from us. I can't see the "250."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You can or cannot, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. Maybe my eyesight is --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If you see in the middle of that big paragraph, and this is both in the English and the B/C/S versions, the middle of paragraph 3, there is a reference to Srebrenica township with some grid references, and then it says: "At least 250 artillery and mortar rounds have been recorded so far." If you like, I have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see. I can see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, do you know what the source of that figure of 250 mortar rounds was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this is -- this should have come from us, as military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as for the other information concerning Dutch-Bat reporting rockets, did that come from you, do you recall, or did that come from Dutch-Bat directly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report that we, ourselves, as Team Srebrenica, were given by Dutch-Bat, and we reported the same. So it came from us, but originally from Dutch-Bat themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving along, sir, may we have 65 ter 491 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you read this okay, sir? I've got a hard copy again, if that's easier for you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what this report is, first?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a situation report, and it is from the sector that is UNPROFOR. It is not by UNMOs; this is the UNPROFOR itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the date and time in the upper left-hand corner, "6 July, 2100 hours, July 1995"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can see the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 1, sir, there is a reference to Potocari compound being targeted several times during the day. Do you see that? It's about the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last sentence in this paragraph indicates that: "In Srebrenica enclave, an artillery impact killed a civilian and injured [Realtime transcript read in error "killed"] a boy." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on your recollection, do you know if these casualties are the same as those you and Major Tetteh observed and reported or are these being reported separately by Dutch-Bat?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a report separately by Dutch-Bat, but I think this is the same as we had observed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look down to the bottom of the page, this is page 2 of the English and we'll have to go to page 3 of the B/C/S, at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. My apologies to you, Mr. Zivanovic. But I was bending down, reading the document, and you just didn't make it further up from the screen, so I never noticed you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a misstatement in the line 15 on the page -- page 15, line 3. It is stated that "killed a boy," but in the original documents, the boy is "injured."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It actually should be reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's reversed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank my friend. It should be reversed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, going down to the bottom of the page, and this is page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, it's paragraph 3(e)(3). There is a reference to the Srebrenica enclave under the heading "Eastern Area." "150 detonations were counted. Due to bunker alarms, an exact figure cannot be given." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, is this information that was being reported from you and Major Tetteh or is this information that Dutch-Bat was gathering on its own and reporting to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this was not our report. This is UNPROFOR, and I guess this figure was given by the Dutch-Bat, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with that document. Thank you. Let's move to the next day of the attack, 7 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what occurred that day? Did the attack continue; and if so, can you describe the shelling that you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the shelling just continued. The following day, it was a continuation of the previous one. The number of shells actually were almost the same, and the target seemed to be the same; that is, Srebrenica itself and Potocari. The pattern followed the same way as the previous day, so there was no let-up on the onslaught. It was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to observe what was actually being struck by the shelling, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, we would get out and after -- that is, after we would get the lull, we would get out, go to the town itself, see where the target was. We were surprised to find that the target mainly was the market area, and surprisingly they were also trying to target the hospital; that is, that was our own conclusion, because you could see they were missing it by a -- by a whisker. Also regarding the PTT building, that we could see because the shells were landing just across, across the river; that is, to a hill which was on the other side. And on the marketplace, at least they were getting -- they were getting the market, but luckily there was nobody in that market. So there were no many casualties, as such, but at least they had some targets they were targeting. Regarding also the roads, the roads - maybe I don't know for what particular reason - but at least they were targeting the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you say they were targeting, for example, the market, what are you referring to, sir? What was being struck?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the -- the shells were landing in the market or just in the vicinity; you know, not necessarily inside, but inside, close by, or somewhere along there. So we could see actually the actual target was that particular -- particular market. And, of course, the market, that is something they all knew its location because it had not changed for a long time. Also, the PTT building was the same for a very long time, and the hospital also.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the hospital and the PTT building, sir. Do you recall whether those were being targeted, from your recollection, that very second day of the shelling or were they targeted later on during the shelling on another day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, even this time, the PTT was being targeted, at least the shells were landing across the other side, but it was never hit. It was never hit during this period at all. Even the hospital was not hit, but we could see the shells were coming somewhere just around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, well, if I remember well, the hospital is practically opposite the PTT building, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was opposite, but you climb a bit to get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So how would you know, as a military man, how would you know whether a shell is aimed at one or is directed to hit one, rather than the other, if they are in the same direct line of shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they're in the same line and they're slightly short of each other, there's some distance in between, you can tell -- if the shell is hitting in between the two buildings, you can tell that maybe it is targeting either. But if it is somewhere maybe of the first building, you can tell that maybe the target was that particular building that is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on the second day of shelling, Colonel, did you or Major Tetteh leave Srebrenica for any reason?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second day, I cannot remember very well, but I think we were called for a meeting. I cannot remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, on either the first or second days of the shelling, do you recall ever going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. We went to Potocari. We were called to Potocari for a meeting with Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall what that meeting was about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was specifically on the issues that had occurred and also to discuss some information that [indiscernible] had received concerning some ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll get to those in a little while. Why don't we look at 65 ter number 492, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is this, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an UNMO report from headquarters, the sector; that is, the Sector BH Northeast to UNMO HQ Command, and also they inform the HQ Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is a daily sitrep for what day, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a daily sitrep for -- it was covering the period 0700 hours. "07," that is the date; and around midnight, that is "0001 Bravo." That is the times that we had there, up to the evening of that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's 2000 hours?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 2000 hours, July 7, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look down at paragraph 3, if we could, and this will be on both the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see where it says: "Team Srebrenica reported that the BSA continued their offensive." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now There is a reference to: "Dutch-Bat reported heavy shelling around their compound in Potocari; and as a result, three men were injured and brought by the MSF to hospital. UNMOs confirm this." Do you recall you or Major Tetteh confirming those injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These were reported to us by Dutch-Bat; and when they were bringing them to hospital, we went there and saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Further on in this paragraph, do you see where it refers to "At 1500, three shells landed in Srebrenica and injured two men. One was picked up by our patrol and the other one by MSF, but he died on arrival at the hospital." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you personally picked up or saw either of these two casualties that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these ones, I cannot remember very well whether I'm the one who picked them or Major Tetteh. I sometimes did not know every issue, but I know of this issue. This is an issue I very well know. We picked them up ourselves and we took them to hospital, but what I can't remember is whether it was me or Major Tetteh.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, moving on, there is a reference to "More shells had been landing in the same spot or around and we suspect they're from a tank positioned at Company Hill. A lot of damage on buildings has been caused in that area, despite the low casualty figure." Now, sir, you referred, yourself, a few moments ago to your surprise, that despite the amount of shelling, there were relatively few casualties. Can you account for that or do you have an explanation, based on your observations, for the relatively low casualty figure at that time, given the amount of shelling that you reported?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think I would say it was quite a surprise to us that there was that kind of heavy shelling; and when you go out, the number of injured -- or rather, the casualties were very few. But we can account this to several facts, and one of them is that the -- the weapons used, these are high-trajectory weapons; that is, the artillery shells, they are high trajectory. Most of the time where they are located, they are somewhere that they can be safe, because these are the major weapons, heavy weapons for a fighting unit. So, first of all, it is to ensure their security. So they would be put behind a hill somewhere or behind a place -- in a place where it is difficult for the enemy to see, and that is from where now you're going to shoot to the other side. We call them"high trajectory," in that they don't aim direct. They go up and then fall on the target or on the place where you have targeted. So sometimes because their target this time is also a valley, because Srebrenica village itself, in fact, the whole place there, they are full of several valleys, hills, and all that. So I think it was a bit difficult to get the actual targets due to that particular fact, that the high trajectory and the target is actually some hills, some valleys somewhere. So it could be difficult to get -- to get the target correctly. So that is a major -- one of the major reasons. Another reason could have been the fact that at least, though maybe not to a large extent, at least we sensitized the people to not go out there during the shelling, to make sure they stay in. I'm not saying that were the ones who did that and that was the main factor. But even themselves, at least they had had more battle than we had, because when the war started in that country, at least they were there. So they knew what to do, and also our assistance maybe helped a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Any other factors that you can accounts for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, you know, other factors at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue looking in this paragraph. There's a reference to "a lot of damage on buildings has been caused." Did you observe damage to buildings, sir, in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing to remember is that most of the buildings in Srebrenica had been hit, one way or the other, during previous onslaughts. But during this one, at least you could go back there and see some fresh -- fresh signs of attack. At least there was fresh damage, not the old damage that you are used to, not the old damage that you knew. So you can easily tell that these buildings have been -- have been hit. There has been something that was hit here because it's a bit fresh. So we could easily see, Your Honour, that they were really destroyed, and it was fresh, not the old destruction that was there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving on, there's a reference at 1700 hours, "21 detonations were heard by UNMOs in Potocari. We suspect they are from an MRL located" at a grid reference," but NCBU." I just want to ask you a couple of questions about that, sir. These 21 detonations heard by UNMOs in Potocari, do you recall whether or not you or Major Tetteh were in Potocari at this time to personally hear these impacts or view their location, or is this something you heard from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- this is information we got from Major De Haan, who was already there in hospital. But at least he could slightly move around, and of course he's -- he as well was working at least. That is not where he had problems. So he heard that and reported to us. He told us and that is what we reported, because it was one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it further states that: "We suspect they are from this multiple rocket-launcher, but NCBU." So what does that qualification there tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The suspicions of where they could be coming from, even if we can get the general direction and it's a certain area, but if you have not confirmed that it is the actual place, then you cannot say you have confirmed. So that's why we put "NCBU," that is, not confirmed by UNMOs. And, Your Honour, this is a place where we knew, in that general area, not in Sarajevo but in one location, there was a rocket-launcher somewhere, located somewhere there, because even before that we used to see rockets, you know, over-flying from that general direction. So we knew there was an MRL somewhere there, but we were not sure. That's why we could not confirm ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "before that," you're referring to prior to the attack which began on 6 July, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how many shells you and Major Tetteh recorded striking Srebrenica town on this second day of shelling, the 7th? Do you recall approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to recall, but definitely it was about 200 -- actually, more than 200, definitely over 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to 65 ter 494 briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a situation report which is sent by Headquarters Sector Northeast. That is being sent to Headquarter UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Covering what period, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time period here is - maybe we can go down here - 1700 hours, that is on the 6th, to 1700 hours on the 7th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a couple of questions, and we'll find out whether that reference to June 1995 is a typo or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2, and this is of both the English and the B B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see, up at paragraph 1: "General Assessment"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we talk about that, do you see a fax transmittal line at the top of the page with a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we might have to scroll to the right on the English version to catch that, please. It will be up at the very upper right of the corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and the dates are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what's the date of the fax transmittal?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 7th of July, 1995, at 2040 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 1 here, it reports that "a BSA tank fired ten rounds at the electricity plant 200 metres southwest of the Potocari compound." Do you recall receiving this information, sir, or hearing about this attack on the electrical plant?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't. I don't remember hearing about the attack on the electricity plant; in fact, I didn't know there was -- there was any.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So from your understanding, then, this information is coming from where?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information, according to what we saw on the previous page, is coming from the -- from UNPROFOR, not military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The next line says: "Due to BSA shelling inside enclave, a total of four civilians killed and 17 wounded." Do you recall the source of this information, first of all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This most likely could have come from Dutch-Bat, but not ourselves, not UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: By the second day of the shelling, do you have any recollection of how many civilians had been wounded and killed by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, I am not very sure. The wounded obviously were many, but the killed -- killed could have been maybe around four, four or somewhere there. I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look further down to section 3 (e 3(e), and we'll have to scroll down on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, under "Eastern Area," there's a reference to the "Srebrenica enclave, 147 detonations." Was this information coming from you or is this from some other source?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not from us. This must have been from the Dutch-Bat, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now let's move to the 8th of July. Can you describe the attack that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8th of July, Your Honour, I think, as far as I can remember, was the heaviest, in terms of shelling, and it started very early and the shelling was concentrated in Potocari itself and Srebrenica village. It was -- I think we counted the most number of shells, and also the damage was enormous. It was, really, I think the heaviest, if I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to 65 ter 495, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an UNMO report from BH Command, Sarajevo, to UNMO headquarter's arrival from UNMO HQ BH Sector Northeast, and it covers the period of July 8, 1995, 1430 hours, July 8, 1995 .

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is described as a "Sit Update." What's that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the normal sitreps were being sent every day in the evening to the cover the whole period of the previous day and that particular day. But whenever something happened that you're required to inform the headquarters, you had to send it as an update. Actually, this is an update to the sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at update number 1: "The shelling started in Srebrenica village this morning at 0800. They seem to be concentrating more on the densely populated areas," two grid references are provided, "and Potocari town." There's a reference to "31 explosions in Potocari and 34 in Srebrenica town, with one landing approximately 20 metres from the UNMO accommodations at 1247." Just reading into that paragraph, sir, do you recall these events?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When it refers to the PTT building and the shrapnel being hurled over it, were you present, sir, for that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was. This was one of the most scaring periods of my stay there, in that. The -- the explosion actually hurled a lot of shrapnel towards our building. Of course, you don't expect us to have any windows, any glass windows, that is true. But some of them tried to penetrate the hard boards that were put in the form of the windows, and we got very scared because we were inside there. The shelling was continuous. Shrapnels have started getting in, and we had nowhere else to go, other than maybe go to the bunker. These really formed a period from where - because at this time we started feeling, ourselves, to be very, very insecure, very insecure - anything could have happened to us any time from that time. Also the PTT, as I said earlier, had some importance to the BSA, in that it had some communications equipment up there. We sensed that maybe they really want to destroy the whole building, and we are no longer safe in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. There's a reference here to the BiH Chief of Staff informing the UNMOs that over 100 shells have landed in a general area described, but this is NCBU. Do you see that, sir? It's in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I've seen this. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, does that indicate just because somebody's reporting something to you, were you able to report it as being confirmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this meant is that we never ignored any information that we got from, whichever source; and, you know, we had reported, we had reported. But if it is something that ourselves have not confirmed, we always made an effort of writing, "Not confirmed by UNMO," so that we can tell whoever this information is going to, ourselves have not confirmed. But at times - in fact, most of the time - we would go out to try to confirm and then that say we have actually confirmed it. But if the circumstances do not allow, it will remain just not confirmed by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. To save some time, I won't ask any more questions about the other portions of this memo, but let me just ask you: As you said, this is a report from your sector headquarters in Tuzla to UNMO BH Command in Sarajevo and Zagreb, but it appears to be an actual copy or verbatim copy of a report from you. It describes "we" and so forth in the text. Can you explain how this -- or how your report is incorporated into these other reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during this, the onslaught on Srebrenica, most of our sitreps and even the updates to the sitreps were being retransmitted the same way we had written, partly because they didn't want to change anything or put any inference by adding or removing anything or trying to report their own way, so that it could have the same impact as we, the originators, could have wanted it to have. Also, maybe due to the time factor, because they wanted this information to reach the upper echelon as soon as possible, and when you try to write it your own way, you waste more time. This was something which was a very serious occurrence, and maybe they wanted the transmission to be very fast. So those were the two main reasons, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe the process by which you and Major Tetteh drafted these reports during this attack, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during this onslaught, what we were doing was that when one observer goes out with one interpreter, the other one would be left behind, trying to put the shell, or rather, to form the report. The data that one comes with the one who has gone on patrol, whatever he comes with, it would just be inserted so that it can be as fast as possible; then when that one comes in and tries to insert that, the other one would go out. So these reports were a coordination of what both of us were getting, and it really did not matter who was writing or sending the report, but it was a summary of what both of us were getting at both different moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, at some point on the 8th of July, did you make an assessment of the food situation in the enclave, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The food situation in the enclave was a serious concern to our headquarters, and this is something that we were doing, I think, almost every week. It was a weekly report on the food situation, and it's not -- not just in Srebrenica. It was everywhere else. This situation was to account for any discrepancies, any additions, so that you can know, in case there are additions to what you expected to have been there, where has it come from? Is it through the normal mafia style? Is it the UNHCR food that is being sold? Is it, you know, for whatever? You've got to know what is really happening, because you've got to have the information on the enclave at your fingertips. So concerning food, we wanted to know whether they steal sufficient food for their people. What about the prices? How high are the prices? Is it still affordable or not? And, of course, on affordability, the people there, you know, we didn't expect them to afford, but at least how affordable is it? How were the curtails working, if any? So those were the main reasons that we were going to check the prices of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned a couple terms there, "mafia" and "cartels," and I'll ask you some follow-up questions in a moment. But, first, during your time in Srebrenica, how would you describe the state of the food supply for the population in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the food in the enclave was coming from UNHCR, the bulk of the food, because those people were dependent on the -- on the UN for food supplies. But in addition to that, as in any situation, be it a war situation, be it a disaster, be it whatever, there are always some people who sometimes try to capitalise on a predicament. And, in this situation, there were people who were trying to go out, which is okay. They go out, buy some food, bring it over to the enclave, sell, and, of course, sell at high prices because en route they had to pay for the BSA soldiers to give them a way through. And when they got back, they've got to sell and get -- and get profits. So this used to happen, and that was their situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the adequacy of the food supply situation in Srebrenica during your time there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was never enough food in Srebrenica, never. There's no time that there was enough food in that -- in that enclave, not at all. Even when UNHCR is there, they could just provide just basic -- the basically required nutritional ingredients, but not enough food for all the people. But at times, you would find some people would try to save some little food here and there from the one that they have been given by the UNHCR, and you find it in the market the following day or two days later. After they have saved a little, it was old, so, finally, they are able to sell a bit of it to the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 493, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir; and if you do, what is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a food report in Srebrenica, and that is being sent from UNMO headquarter in Sarajevo to UNMO headquarter, Zagreb, and this was done on the 8th at 930 hours, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who prepared this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report would have come from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall how you went about compiling this report on the 8th of July, during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember very well, in that we went out there and, you know, we had small, small shops that used to sell a bit of food. And also around the market area, some were there, the people who were selling and who could be able to get the prices. You know, it was like sampling. You know, you just go there and get an item. If it is wheat flour, if it is anything, whatever item that you find there, you ask the price of those who were buying and those who were selling, because sometimes there could be some difference. Some could lie that, "We bought it for this much"; whereas, actually they were sold at a higher price, or vice versa. So we went out there and got these from the people themselves, those who were selling and those who were buying, and that is what we used to compile this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the market was one of the areas that appeared to you to be targeted, so why were there still people available for you to even interview?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in every situation, there would always be people somewhere there. Even during the tsunami, there were still people selling and buying. So you ask me that, sometimes I cannot even understand myself, but they were there. You find they are there. You told them not to be there, but they would still be somewhere. And we got them and they give us their prices; and also, as I say, there were some shops nearby, small, small shops, which were selling these commodities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to page 2, please, and this is in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 3, and I won't dwell on this, it speaks for itself, where did you get this information regarding the UNHCR planned deliveries?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, for UNHCR, this one, normal, normal convoys, and we used to know when they are scheduled to bring in food supplies, fuel supplies, to the enclave, and they were scheduled. We used to know about them. We had to know about them so that we could also arrange for security, their own security, during the transit. In fact, they were relying on us observers to ensure security. Also, there was need, at that particular moment, because they had been denied entry earlier. So there was definitely a shortage of food. So everyone was concerned about this UNHCR convoy, and this was the main lifeline for the whole enclave. So every UNHCR was being greeted with a lot of joy. So this was something we were following throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look down to paragraph 4 regarding the water supply, was this water supply information new to you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not new. This was not new to us, because this is something that was there throughout. What was being gotten from some springs, this was more hygienic than the main river. Because from the spring, you expect it to come in fresh from the hill. So there were some points where UNHCR had constructed a pipe to gather water from in there, so that people can draw it from outside, and it used to work very well. For people going there, they would line up, and you could see a line of 100 metres of people waiting with their container to go there so that they can draw water. So this was nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where did you get your water, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our water, we had two sources; that is, normal drinking water. We were getting it from that compound. So we had to send a patrol every day to go to Dutch-Bat, draw the water in our drums, small, small drums, small containers, bring it over to the -- to our building. So that is the one that we used to cook with and also to drink. Now, the other water for washing our clothes and the building, that is, the offices and all that, came from those -- those wells or sometimes the rivers themselves. It didn't have to be very clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, moving down to paragraph 7, this is on page 2 of the English and on page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was this electricity information new to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not new. This is what these girls were using. They were improvising their own electricity, in that what they were doing is they were diverting from the main river. Let's say, from a small hill up there, they would divert it directly through a certain gradient and all of a sudden increase the gradient so it could drive some turbines down there. That would, in the normal process, generate electricity. Using the normal river flow, it could help generate and transmit electricity. So that was normal. But this kind of electricity, for one, is not safe, and also reliability is not assured, but it was there. They were using that, in fact even for this electricity, they were using for some video shops to show movies and some other small, small activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you power your equipment, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were operating them using a generator, which is diesel-driven. And somehow when there was no diesel or when the supply was low, we had to change the timings, in that like during this period, we were just starting the generators when we have something to do, when we have a report to write, not for anything else. Because the supply was low, none of the convoys were being allowed in, so we had to change our pattern of operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let's move to the 9th of July. You described the 8th of July as being the heaviest. How did the 9th progress, in terms of shelling, and does anything stand out in your mind about any decisions you made that day, the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th obviously started just like the other days. Unfortunately, I think this is the day that we later noticed a tank had come close-by, and the hit of a tank is normally direct. It's not high trajectory like the artillery. So this one hits direct, and we got very scared. We knew our place now targeted, and they could get us any time they wanted. So I think this was a major, major turning point in our stay in Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that we are about two minutes from the break, but rather than calling a document, if we could take the break a little earlier, I think that will work better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Thayer. Let's have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where's the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We asked for just a couple moments for a quick preliminary with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: First, to give the Chamber an idea of timing with respect to this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are anxious to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sure, and we understand the urgency of time. We share that. I've been trying to cut the direct as much as I can. Things, nevertheless, are moving actually slower than I had expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's our feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So I and everybody, I think, shares that and understands that. Unfortunately, that means that I think I should be able to conclude the direct today. I've canvassed my friends to see if, based on my direct, the potential cross might have been cut at all. Sometimes that's the case. If I do a fairly thorough direct, it cuts down on cross-examination questions. My understanding is, given how contested this witness's testimony is, we expected it to be so, and I think it has proven to be so, the cross estimates have not changed. So there is, I think, very little way, under any circumstances, that we are going to be able to finish this witness's testimony before the recess. Prior to him taking the stand, I'd actually inquired about his availability to return, if the Court permitted, in January. His schedule is wide open, so he is available to do that, Your Honours. So we wanted to keep the Court aware of those developments. I think Mr. McCloskey may be prepared later. I don't know now if this is the appropriate time now to update the Court on the Dean Manning issues, in terms of tendering and some agreements which may or may not be finalised. But I wanted to bring those two matters to the Court's attention and give you a realistic idea of where things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It sounds like an unfinished symphony to me. You finish your direct today, if I understood you well, or you should be in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think I should be in a position to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Tomorrow, I think some of my friends will be in a position to start. I don't know if they are unified on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't know if they're unified on a position as to whether beginning cross and then interrupting cross for his return is something they wish to do. That I'm not certain of, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether we're all uniform, but at least five Defence teams believe that it would be more appropriate to start the cross-examination after the break because our cross will be interrupted. Another reason is that we were informed by the Prosecutor, in the proofing note, that the witness is -- has a certain number of documents which he will give the Prosecutor once he comes back his the country. And since these are UNMO reports, we believe it would be more appropriate that we start the cross when we have seen the documents which the witness holds for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which documents does the witness hold for the time being that the Defence haven't seen?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are documents that neither of the parties have seen. One is a notebook which he maintained, which he said contains some not detailed notes of events, including the events during the attack, which he took at the time, which he had with him during his 1997 OTP interview, but which was not copied. I inquired whether he had that. He indicated he did, and he would furnish us a copy. The other documents are some copies of Srebrenica team reports that were sent to Tuzla during the time. He had destroyed all of -- as far as he knew, all of the original UNMO -- his original copies of UNMO reports from Srebrenica to Tuzla before the Dutch-Bat withdrawal out of concern for his safety should they be discovered. He realised that a couple copies had come out with him interspersed among his equipment. He has copies of those at home. I asked him if he would provide those to us. I asked him whether there was, to his understanding and recollection, anything in those reports that hasn't already been captured or is actually present in the various attachments to his OTP witness statement, which formed the basis of these reports that are being shown to him now. He said that he did not believe that there was anything knew or different in those reports. As you heard him say, what Tuzla was doing with his reports was simply re-transmitting them to Zagreb or BH Command at Sarajevo. So what we are seeing are, in some cases, verbatim copies of these reports that came from Team Srebrenica, of which he has, he said, a handful of copies at home, but there's nothing knew in those, as far as he knows. So I don't think there's going to be anything new or surprising in either of these documents, but we will have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And who are the five Defence teams that are united in preferring to start the cross-examination after the holidays or the recess? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I'm not sure who the five are and I think they can announce it for themselves, but we're one of them. It is only because I think, although my learned friend calls it a notebook, I think the witness identified it as a diary, and he kept two sets of diary, from my understanding. Also, he's writing a book, and we would like and we would ask the Court to get that transcript. I understand that it's almost complete, and it does involve the events relating to Srebrenica in 1995. So we would ask that those documents be presented to us. And if it is a diary, as I understand that it is, it was my understanding he kept it contemporaneous with the events, and it may be relevant for all of us here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you're one of the five. I suppose Madame Fauveau is also amongst that group. I saw Mr. Zivanovic anxiously on his feet. You want to join the five?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would join, just to the submission of Madame Fauveau and Mr. Ostojic, that I asked additional documents from the Prosecution, but they need Rule 70 clearance. Mr. Thayer has informed about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't heard about those yet. Madam Nikolic, are you also amongst the five?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I join my colleagues; although, my cross-examination will be far shorter and maybe even reduced to nothing after having heard their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we are among these five Defences who would like to join Madame Fauveau's submission. To be honest, I really cannot know at this point what is the relevance of the documents that are in the possession of the witness. I cannot exclude that it could be relevant, or any other solution. I mean, I just cannot be sure about it, and I really wouldn't be -- wouldn't feel comfortable in starting my cross-examination and then later receive some documents which could lead in a completely different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is coming back in any case, so you can then put fresh questions. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we weren't aware that this submission was going to be made, so I can't claim that the Gvero team were part of the five. Frankly, our position is we wish to maintain our position on the indictment. We made it clear to learned friends at an earlier point in the case that that's what we wanted to hitherto. This was some months ago. And whilst I don't, as such, support what's being said; in reality, I suppose I must, because if they're going to get their extra time, then inevitably we will, because we want to go sixth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa? Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We join the application. We are agreed that the cross should start in January rather than now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reasons stated by Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not just solidarity?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not just solidarity. We simply believe that we can save some time in not explaining everything that's already been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We need to discuss amongst ourselves, obviously, and take a decision, which we will let you know about later on. Yes, about the documents that require the Rule 70 clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I can clarify a couple of the references that were made. My friend, Mr. Zivanovic, had made a specific request for any of the original Srebrenica-to-Tuzla UNMO reports coming from Team Srebrenica. We did a database search and couldn't find any of those original documents. And in connection with that, I inquired of the witness as to whether he had any. That's when I understood that he had a couple of those originals that he had brought out with him inadvertently. During the course of the review, I located some Sector Northeast, that is, Tuzla, daily sitreps and some other related documents that date back to May through the end of July that were never shown to the witness Kingori. It didn't have his name on it, which I had seen for the first time. Out of an abundance of caution, I asked my friend if he wished to have access to those. He indicated he did. Since we've never sought to use them, we didn't have Rule 70 clearance, so we've had to apply for those. Those are the documents that we're referring to there. Again, those aren't original Srebrenica. As far as I know, they cover time periods outside of this immediate 6 through 18 July time period. There may be some that are inside in there, but again that's a separate request. This is the first time I am hearing about any book that this witness may be working on. I understand my friends met with the witness over the weekend. I've not heard anything about that. I don't see the relevance of a book. That sounds to me like it's been written after the fact. Unless he's got additional contemporaneous documents, then I don't see the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's something we can discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, but it's the first I'm hearing about it, Mr. President, as well. With respect to the actual notebook that I referred to, I've never heard it referred to as a diary. In fact, there were two notebooks he kept contemporaneously, the first which he said was much more detailed in terms of the activities he witnessed, the meetings that happened. He destroyed that prior to the Dutch-Bat withdrawal, again out of his concern for his safety. He destroyed the notebook that contained the more detailed, as he described it, incriminatory information of whomever. The second notebook, which is the one he still has, as I said, he described as much less detailed. That included just a record of sometimes firing incidents or brief descriptions of meetings. That he felt safer to be taken out. That's the one we're referring to, but I haven't heard it as a personal diary. That's the first I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, no offence meant to you, Mr. Thayer, if I am bypassing you, but we also want to make sure that all the time, while you are making these statements, that you are aware of the fact, and that you still remember what we told you earlier on this week, that you have a deadline for resting your case which will not be moved. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I am very conscious of that and the Court's position on that, and I can give you a little update on where our discussions with the Defence have been on some ongoing things. I think the Defence would like that I did that as well. It would just take a minute or two. As you know, Alistair Graham is still out there as a witness, and I think we have a stipulation - we especially worked with the Borovcanin team - about a few issues relating to his that his testimony. We don't think any feels it is necessary to call him back, unless you do. So that should be taken care of. We should have that stipulation, if we're lucky, before the break. There's also a videographer of the Scorpion film, and we have a stipulation worked out on that. So that person won't be -- won't have to be called. Now, in regarding Dean Manning's exhibits, we're in the midst of that, but it appears that the Defence is not objecting to many of the reports that he based his earlier work on: The fabric analysis, the shell casing analysis, the soil/pollen analysis. They, as you know, are objecting now to the DNA material which was the subject of his last report; and because of that, as you know, I think I've mentioned before, we will need - unless you think otherwise - need to bring in someone from the ICMP to give a foundation for the methods and procedures upon which this material is based. I hope not to bring in someone to talk about chromosomes and how DNA is matched and that kind of thing; though, I think the witness will have basic knowledge of that. I think we're long past the need for that kind of thing. But as for the methods and procedures and how they take the blood and match the families to the missing, based on the challenge, I think it's appropriate that we bring that in so you can see that. We had not thought we'd have to, frankly, because we got no objection from Helge's -- Helge Brunborg's report that had that significant information in it, and Helge Brunborg described the basic methods and procedures. But now that Mr. Manning has relied on some of that and we have this objection, we're in the process of trying to organise that ICMP witness to come sometime after -- after Mr. Butler. Along with that, we may need to bring in a brief demographics witness, because the date we get from the ICMP is in a raw form that our demographics person applies so that we can make sense of it for Dean Manning and Helge. We may be able to reach a stipulation on that, but that may -- those two witnesses may be some that we have to bring together. As I think you invited me to do, we will file a motion requesting those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This leads me also to another thing. You have filed a confidential motion to add another witness to your list, which would occupy, I think, a good day or two if he is brought over. Is there a position taken by the Defence teams on that motion, because we need to know. I mean, otherwise, we will, tomorrow, we will have to sit. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should be a very short witness, as the motion says, in terms of the Prosecution's direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what his testimony is going to be like, so you are in a better position to make an assessment than we are. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to say something concerning the latest motion you've just mentioned. I believe it is too early to express our position, since Mr. Pandurevic's lead counsel is not here, and I wish to meet him first before responding to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
