utterances.text: Yes, but I would imagine Mr. Haynes would have made up his mind by now, and Mr. Sarapa would certainly be privy to that information. That's what the co-counsel is here for, or one of the reasons. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the witness that is being proposed, I would kindly ask that we state our position after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After the next break, that is, after 12.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as you can tell, we have been in discussions with the Defence about various things. They've asked us, on our position, for an extension of the -- I think they'll be asking you for extensions of a couple of the deadlines that you have set, and we've provided them our viewpoint on that, based on some of the things that they were able to agree with us and save us some time. So I would put that in their hands, as they, I think, know our position, and I can respond as well. But I think everyone wanted to get that out to you so you could see what the parties were feeling before the holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I think that was limited only to the time period or the limit fixed by us for the filing of the 65 ter documents, not any other extension. That's how I understood it from Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You are correct, and what we needed is we saw that we needed additional time for the preparation. The Court did set the date of March 31st, and we wanted to know the position of the Prosecution, if we could move that deadline up to and through April 30th. I believe we have an agreement on that, or at least no objection, and we're just going to inquire of the Court, with your permission, if we could amend that order so that the deadline for the 65 ter witness list and documents be presented by April 30th. Another condition to the agreement or non-objection that we have is my learned friend from the OTP requested that we, at the very least, provide to him the military experts only by the 31st of March, as the Court had earlier set as the deadline, and we have agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. It seems to me, in my mind, that you're trying to reach a package deal between and amongst yourselves. If that is the case, we also have another point to make; and if necessary, we'll incorporate it in an appropriate order. But we are giving you an advance notice of it, just as we did prior to the Prosecution -- to the opening of the trial and the start of the Prosecution case. We'll be calling upon you, the Defence teams, to submit a list of possible agreed facts and adjudicated facts on which stipulation from the Prosecution could be forthcoming. So this is also an exercise that and which would perhaps justify delaying a little bit the filing date limit for 65 ter purposes. But, anyway, I know, but forgive me, because sometimes the column stands in the way. It seems as if it's moving. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. My apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Ostojic. Just to clarify, we don't have an objection to a 30-day extension for the witness list and the exhibit list; though, we would like them to stick by your order related to the experts and their reports, so we get all of those, you know, at once upon the deadline you set, otherwise -- military experts. The other experts can get the 30 days as well. I think they have demographics and other things which -- which we've agreed that that's all right to give them the 30 days as well. Also, I'm sure you will recall that Mr. Ostojic and I were having discussions about the US aerial imagery issues with the US, and we have reached an agreement on that. That issue is no longer something we need to present to you; though, Mr. Ostojic is still objecting to those images, which of course is fine by us. But we don't feel a need to get the US involved anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the only pleasure yet to come for today, for the time being, is Mr. Sarapa's announcement after the break. Okay. Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, please -- sorry. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just mention this: The Gvero team filed a motion yesterday which I see has not yet reached certainly my system, which may, in some small way, impact on the time issue, and clearly the Chamber and the Prosecution will need to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not aware of it as yet, so If you have a copy that you could let us have as a courtesy copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a reason it's not on the system. There was a bureaucratic problem, but I'm grateful to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't know there were bureaucratic problems in this Tribunal. It's the first time I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I seem to be particularly prone to them, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before the break, you were describing the events of the 9th of July and the proximity of a tank to your position in the town of Srebrenica. Can you describe what decisions you made and what caused those decisions that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe, maybe one correction. I'm seeing it's been written "Josse," but I'm Joseph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is a different person.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a different person. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. On the 9th, I think what happened was the proximity of the tank was so threatening to us and so intimidating, we found it unsafe to continue staying there. What I was saying before the break is that the tank fires directly. It is unlike the artillery which is high trajectory. So this would definitely get a direct hit if it strikes. So we were afraid that we would be targeted and hit without -- without any heads up, and we felt the best thing to do was for us to leave our place, that is, the PTT building, and go to a place that we felt could have been slightly safer, and that is Potocari, that is, the Dutch-Bat compound. So we talked, we had a meeting. We requested for a meeting from the deputy mayor so that he can give us permission or allow us to leave the -- our PTT building. The reason for this, it may look a bit funny that we were asking for permission, but we felt intimidated by the presence of some armed BiH soldiers out of the building moving around. Also there were lots of civilians, very many civilians, who are around the PTT building, and also the Bravo Company, that is, the big company of the Dutch-Bat that was just around there. We felt it is proper for us to tell these people to ensure that we have a safe exit from that place on the way to the Dutch-Bat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this -- this person who you recall was the deputy mayor?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think his name was Osman Suljic or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe the meeting you had with him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We held two meetings, Your Honour, with him. The first one was earlier on, when we requested that we be allowed to leave; and he said, in no uncertain terms, that we cannot leave that place, we cannot leave Srebrenica, because he believed if we leave, that will be the end of the enclave. The BSA will have an open field. They will be able to do whatever they want without fear of being reported by us. So they felt we should carry on staying there until maybe something is done to revise the situation. Then we reported the same to our -- our headquarters, and they told us to continue requesting them. They told us to diplomatically try to persuade them to allow us to leave, and this now we did later in the day. We talked to him, together with his other people, the other people that he had, through persuasion, and also through trying to tell him that, sincerely, even if we stay there and we are hit, surely no one would be reporting about the issues that happen after that. And, in fact, I would like to inform you that he actually broke down into tears and asked us, "Surely, you want to leave us alone like this for the Serbs to do whatever they want to us? Do you really want to go to a safe place and leave us unsafe here?" We told him that sincerely, even when we went to the Dutch-Bat compound, we still continue reporting the same way and trying to tell the headquarters or the UN whatever issues are happening or going on in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So who went with you from Srebrenica to Potocari, and can you describe your trip there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we - it was me and David Tetteh and also one interpreter, that is, Emir, Emir Suljagic - after we were given permission to leave by the deputy mayor, we packed the few items we could manage to get, put them in the Jeep. I personally drove that Jeep all the way to Potocari, and it's worth informing you that it was very scary. It was a very scary trip. In fact, we didn't know that we would survive that trip. It was a short distance, about seven kilometres or so, but it looked like a thousand kilometres, in that there was shelling on our way out and the shells could land on either side of the road near our vehicle; that is, as we were moving, the shells could land sometimes ahead of us, sometimes behind us. But luckily they were hitting softer ground, that is, where there was rice planted and wheat or whatever, and the -- I mean, there were no shrapnels going up to hit us. So we managed, and I was driving at a speed of about 90 kilometres, in gear number three, to engage all those corners and also so that I could be able to stop the vehicle in case of any emergency. So it was very, very scary all the way up to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The other interpreter who you identified as Hasan, do you know where he was when you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Hasan was there with us. He was around there somewhere. He was looking for his -- his people. And when we said that we want to go to Potocari, he said he cannot leave that place until he finds his relatives, who he said were everywhere. He didn't know where they were, and he was scared he might -- they might get killed or whatever. So he said he cannot go with us. We left him in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately, we arrived in the Dutch-Bat compound; in fact, we felt a sigh of relief. We went into an old business of establishing communication with our headquarters. We had to set up our communication; and, immediately, we informed our headquarters that we already now relocated to Dutch-Bat compound in Potocari and that now they can transmit to us without any -- any problems. Then, later on, we thought of how we can be able to know the situation in Srebrenica, and we had to make a decision on how to go about the business of Srebrenica itself, that is, the town, and also the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What decision did you come to, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, we really had very few, very few options, very few options, because we felt we might be unable to go back there ourselves, and that driving our jeep up there could have been very unsafe. So we talked. We talked and agreed that we can send one of our observers, that is, the one we had, Emir Suljagic, so he could go up there and maybe monitor the situation for us and tell us what clearly is happening. We felt he might be safer than us at that particular moment because he's a local, and maybe no one may know who he is and he may still be able to communicate with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I just notice that in the transcript, it indicates that "We talked and agreed that we can send one of our observers," and you refer to Emir. He was a translator, just to be clear, interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He was a -- I don't know whether we wrote a "observer," but he's actually not our observer. He was our interpreter, yellow card.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what time of the day did he, in fact, head back to Srebrenica, sir, and do you know how he got there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he moved out later in the evening under the cover of darkness, and he moved along -- along the river, which was behind the Dutch-Bat compound, all the way up, you know, through concealment, all the way up to Srebrenica town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to then communicate with him, sir; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had given him one of our handsets, so that when he arrives there, he can be able to talk to us, he can be able to communicate with us using the handset.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. I want to show you a couple of reports that were sent out on the 9th, one before -- a couple before your withdrawal, and then we'll pick up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter number 498, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is a sitrep; in fact, it's is an update from UNMO headquarter, Sector Northeast, to UNMO headquarter, Sarajevo, in Zagreb. But as they are saying here it is actually direct from to our team, and they have put it the way we had written it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I notice there's an abbreviation "TA" after "UNMO Team Srebrenica." What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Tango Alpha. That is a team. That is a code name for Team Sebrenica. Every team had different code names, like "Tango Sierra" was Team Sebrenik; "Tango Alpha" was Team Sebrenica; and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving to the document, sir, the second paragraph starts: "The morning started beautifully and we thought all would remain well, but that changed at 800 hours when shelling started in Srebrenica again." It also states that "UNMOs have also counted up to 113 explosions in both Sebrenica and Potocari." Where is that information coming from, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this information comes from us. We're the ones who were reporting it. And like that of Srebrenica, even from Potocari, we could be able to hear what was happening, the shelling and all that; though, the -- our yellow card is Emir, and he could tell us from Srebrenica itself. But also we could hear maybe the actual place where they hit. We could clarify it was this such-and-such a place, but the counting we could be able to do it ourselves also.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. At the time of this report, which is 1440 hours, were you still in Srebrenica, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is at 1440, 1440. Yeah, I think 1440 we were still in Srebrenica. I think -- I think we left at -- at 1800 hours or so from Srebrenica to Potocari, so this was from us directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at some other documents and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving on further in that paragraph, sir, there's a reference to on the 8th of July, at 2240 hours. Do you see that? "UNMOs observed many persons entering Srebrenica town from Slapovic, Swedish shelter village, and neighbouring villages. Some are seeking shelter from relatives, while others are staying in the school compound." Did you personally observe this influx, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was on the 8th, so we actually observed it ourselves. We saw people coming in, streaming in from the Swedish shelter village. This was a village outside Srebrenica where refugees had been sheltered. It was a government, a Swedish government, initiative to build houses for these people, and they started streaming in down to Srebrenica because they felt that was a safer place for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we turn to page 2 of the English, and this will be page 3 of the B/C/S of this document. We'll need to scroll down on the English, and I think we can stay where we are for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a difficult document to locate portions in. But if you could look about two-thirds of the way down the document, there's a reference to one of the public officials from Srebrenica requesting security from Dutch-Bat for the local hospital. Do you see that portion, sir? It may be easier if you look up from the bottom: "MSF, however, refused such a security, explaining that any military presence in and around the hospital would attract military confrontation which would be detrimental to the sick."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you present at that discussion, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the request that Dutch-Bat send soldiers there actually was turned down. Especially they felt, certainly myself felt, that the sending soldiers there would make the hospital a lucrative object for the BSA to attack. So instead of it being a target of the BSA attack, they felt the best thing is to leave it like that, and also because normally the hospitals are not supposed to have soldiers. Internationally, and due to the Geneva Convention, those who are in there are either people wounded or injured, and so no one is supposed to attack a hospital. So you make sure and you just ensure that there are not soldiers around, so that you don't make it a lucrative target for the -- for the other guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, from this period of the 6th of July until the time you withdrew to Potocari, did you have an opportunity to actually enter this hospital; and if so, for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I had an opportunity to enter the hospital; although, that was not the first time I entered. But at least at this particular time I entered because we were told that there were people who had been taken there who were injured. I think - I can't recall very well - that there was one who was -- who died or something like that. So I went there to check what was happening at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall personally transporting or bringing any wounded to the hospital, yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, several, several. I think I made one or two trips to that -- to that hospital. That was almost every day. But on this particular day, I remember taking some to that hospital, wounded ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, based on your observations inside the hospital, was there anything there to indicate that this was being used as a military facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, inside that hospital, I don't think there was anywhere that was being used as a -- as a military base or hardware store, military hardware store or something, because I went round. I remember I went round to check the condition of the other guys who were wounded, and really you could not see anywhere where there was evidence of -- of soldiers or arms or even a store for anything that was military. I could not -- I remember not seeing anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another report from that day, 65 ter 499, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you identify what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a situation update from UNMO headquarter, Sector Northeast, directed to UNMO headquarter, BH Command, and also Zagreb, and this was on the 9th at around 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The report indicates that between 1400 hours and 1516 hours, that your team reportedly heard 78 explosions in Srebrenica town alone and that more than 70 per cent of the explosions were in the center of town. You've testified that in the previous days, you'd heard hundreds of detonations and that you had been counting them. Was there anything particular or anything in particular about this shelling that was different?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the only peculiar issue here is the concentration of the firepower was a bit too high in one particular grid square; that is, Charlie Papa 6385. These were very scary to us, in that when you find a concentration of firepower in one area, there must be something that really they want to soften. There must be something that they want to get out of that place. That was the only reason why we felt this is a bit different from the others, because the others we could hear from different areas, you know, a wide range of weapons coming, you know, or hitting very many different areas. But now this was a concentration on one area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately where, in the center of town, this grid location was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot, but I think this was, I think, the market or near the hospital. I'm not very clear in my mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on in this report, it states that: "They also reported hearing some small-arms fire within their location." Was that small-arms fire incoming or outgoing, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are small-arms fire incoming from the BSA side, not from the BiH side; and maybe it's good to know how you identify incoming fire and outgoing fire. It's very easy to know fire which is coming in, in that the origin where the weapon is -- the fire is coming from, the kind of noise that you hear from that direction is not the same as the hit that you hear after the bullet has hit a certain area. It's not the same, and we are able to easily identify that kind of fire. Also, if it does not hit that particular area, you hear a whizzing noising that is going past, and you definitely know towards which the direction it's heading to. So if you can hear the direction it's heading to, definitely you would be able know the direction that it's coming from. So it was very easy to know that it was incoming fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the fact that it was incoming fire, sir, was that significant to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is significant because you find normally, after you have softened the target by using artillery, be it even tanks or even air power, the next thing that you do is to go and mop up the place. That is where normally we tell the army that is where they go after -- after the air power has already softened the target. And in this case, it was artillery and the tank power. So the infantry now, maybe, we thought, now this is the time they are coming in to mop up the place, that is, to clear, in fact to come in to hold. Actually, the right word is to hold the ground. So that is now the last phase, because after they come to hold the ground, they must dig a defensive position so that now they can defend it against any counter-attack. So these to us showed like it's now going toward the final phase of the onslaught.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how, if at all, did that contribute to your decision to withdraw from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, considering the range of small arms, it's not like the artillery where you can say 2.5 kilometres or even beyond two kilometres and all that. For the small arms, the longest range that you can get, even from an AK-47, I think an AK-47 is about 600 metres. Other rifles can go up to 900 metres or even call it 1.000 metres, that is, one kilometre. So one kilometre is very close, that is very close. And when he's somewhere there, he can scare you, and he definitely will be moving more towards you and he will get you. Small arms, definitely, when someone is in range and you are not harmed, surely he will definitely kill you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that when you're not armed. As an UNMO, sir, - and I may have asked you this, but forgive me if I didn't - were UNMOs armed during their service, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, UN military observers all over the world, they're never armed. They -- normally, the only arms that they have is a good and working pen and a notebook. Then, obviously, you can have a flak-jacket to protect yourself. But the weapons normally that we have is a pen and a book to write.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now let's look to the 10th of July, sir. Just one quick question. Where did you spend the night of the 9th, physically?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, physically we spent the night in the Dutch-Bat compound. We got ourselves a container that was a bit free. We removed some items, and that is where we slept for the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we look at 65 ter number 502, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what this is, sir; and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an UNMO report being sent from UNMO HQ Zagreb, Sector Northeast, to Zagreb and BH Command. It is a situation update from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this is on the 10th of July. Let's just move to point 3 to save a little bit of time. It indicates that: "Reports, via phone from the team, report that the shelling is ongoing in the area of Srebrenica town." How is that information coming from Srebrenica, given that you're in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the shelling could be heard from any position, especially if you are along that main road leading from Bratunac all the way to Srebrenica. So we were hearing the shelling. Also in our report, our interpreter, Mr. Emir, was also in that place, and he could talk to us and tell us where the shelling is actually going on. But at least even ourselves from Potocari, we could be able to hear and count.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, focusing on the 10th of July, sir, do you recall, in particular, any other information that Emir was transmitting to you from Srebrenica that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for the -- for the shelling, he could tell us the actual hit, the actual place where the shells were hitting; and also concerning the injured, if any, and the dead, if any. Actually, the actual condition or situation in Srebrenica, he could be able to tell us from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 501, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to move things along, this is dated the 10th of July, 1025 hours. At number 1, we can see that it's being retransmitted as received from you through Tuzla to UNMO Command in Zagreb and UNPROFOR -- or UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the entry at 1230 hours, there's a reference to over 100 detonations, and then at 0930, about eight rockets being fired in the direction of Srebrenica. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how these two reports were confirmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, for the -- for the 100 detonations, obviously we counted ourselves. Now, for the -- for the rockets, the eight rockets, obviously they were fired from -- the report came from Dutch-Bat, and so we reported the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect, for example, to the hundred detonations that you said you could count yourself, what confirmation, if any, from Srebrenica did you receive about those detonations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the confirmation from Srebrenica was coming from our yellow card, that is, Emir, and also we could be able to count ourselves. We could count, but also he was confirming to us it was exactly hitting Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've referred a couple of times to the term "yellow card." What does that mean or refer to, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yellow card" was the identification card that was being given to all interpreters. So we easily refer to them as "yellow cards," and especially when you don't want to come out clear. In military terms, you don't want to come out clear when you're talking on the set. So when you say "yellow card," you know you mean the interpreter, but someone else may not understand. In fact, it is meant to do what exactly what he has done to you, so that you may not understand what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference to a tank, a BSA tank, making the recovery of some UNPROFOR APCs very difficult. What, if anything, did you learn about this event?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, there was, you know, in the enclave we had several observation posts which were manned by -- by Dutch-Bat. I think there were about ten or more observation posts. These are posts which are outside the normal area and where you really want to observe to know what is happening around that place, so that you can also report. And also in case of any rapid requirement of force, those people at the OP can be able to react immediately. So that was, first and foremost, their sense of the OPs. It also helped us observers to go there and observe from there. Now, for this particular location, there was a tank, a BSA tank somewhere, and it was located. It was sighted. The -- the OP that was there, they felt they wanted to withdraw, but they cannot because of the fear of that -- of that tank. It was actually intimidating. To them, it was intimidating, so it was very difficult for them to start that, to start moving, because they feared they could have been hit. It was a lot of fear because you can see it. They can see you. So you don't know the next course of action that you should take.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you received any information about the APC or any other vehicle being fired upon by -- by that tank?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that I cannot -- I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, sir. If we look down at the next sitrep update at 1255 hours, it indicates that: "Two heavy shells, probably 155-millimetre artillery shells, hit the direct surrounding of the hospital at 1100 hours. All the windows are smashed and shrapnel has showered the walls and rooms of the hospital." Do you recall who reported that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was reported by the -- by Emir, and this is what he sent to us from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as far as you've stated, Emir is a -- an interpreter. Do you have any knowledge, based on your working with him, what position he was in to assess this as a 155-millimetre artillery shell? You qualify it as "probably" in the report, but why is that even being mentioned as a 155-millimetre artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the experience these interpreters had in that place was very high, having been there for around three years or so, and having worked with various observers, and also having been responsible or having been able to assist us to analyse the craters when we were there, and all the other observers, you know, make them have an upper hand. In fact, they could have been more experienced by newer -- more than newer observers in the field of analysing some of these things, in that they were there throughout. And at least with the technicalities, they could be able to tell a shell. They could be able to distinguish sometimes even between a mortar -- a mortar shell and an artillery shell. So the experience that they had and the way we had worked with them, we could know that they can tell us an actual situation, the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter 503, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we're looking at a re-transmission, as it says here, of Srebrenica update at 1346 hours on the 10th. It indicates that Srebrenica township is still undergoing a very heavy shelling. The report states that: "We have recorded figures, 49 shells between 1250 and 1533 hours and nine rockets launched into the town ..." Again, with respect to the shelling, where is that information coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, for the shelling, as I had said earlier, the shelling, we could count the shells landing anywhere between Potocari and Srebrenica. From Potocari, we could be able to count the number of shells, and also now our yellow card there could now be able to confirm that actually this is true. So we could easily tell; that is, for the shells. For the rockets, as I said, most of the rockets were originating from a hill somewhere near Bratunac, to the -- to the west of Bratunac, somewhere there. So those ones we could even see them over-flying Potocari, so it was very easy to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say "we," you mean yourself, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we, the military observers, because that is me and David Tetteh. And, already, at this time, Andre De Haan is there with us, though fully not recovered, but he was there. When I say "we," I mean military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, sir, do you have a recollection personally of ever seeing rockets over-flying Potocari from that direction you just described towards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not once. At least I have, I can remember personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "not once," sir, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rockets did not fly -- over-fly Potocari once. There were several times that we noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 505 displayed on e-court, please. If we could go to page 3 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S, please. If we could focus down on the entry for 1645 hours on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, here the report refers to the yellow card reporting various information. At the bottom, number 4 refers to: "Latest information received reports of the following villages being burnt by the BSA," and it lists one village. I'm afraid our -- the copy that we managed to obtain stops there. But with respect to that report, do you recall where that information was coming from, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this information came from the people who were streaming into Srebrenica and also all the way down to -- to Potocari. This is the information that they were bringing, and especially those who were, first of all, arriving in Srebrenica. Our yellow card could be able to tell us what this is what they are saying and this is what, I think, the condition on the ground is. So we were reporting the way -- the way they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I just noticed, if you look at this page, there are a series of situation updates, all dated the 10th of July at various times.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the top of the page, please, I just wanted to clarify one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It refers, you can see it at the upper right-hand corner, "Annex A, dated 09 July." Is it fair to say that's probably a typo, given all these events occurred on the 10th, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a typo error. As part of these things, they are always there, and so we just put the update and sometimes one may forget to change the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with that document; thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, that brings us to the 11th of July. Do you recall attending a meeting, Colonel, in the very, very early morning hours of July 11th; and if so, can you share with the Trial Chamber who was there and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a meeting called very early in the morning, and this was by Colonel Karremans, I think, the CO Dutch-Bat, and the BiH. As I recall, I think the essence of the meeting was to convey some messages to -- to the BiH and also to hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember, in particular, anything that was discussed or any information that was given or transmitted in particular during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this meeting, there was an issue concerning -- mainly, there were two issues, I think. One of them was concerning the -- the BSA, I think, giving -- I think there were two ultimatums being given, and I think the BSA had conveyed a message that they would like the Muslims to leave the enclave. They'll be given a safe passage to get out. Also, I think there was an issue of -- of an air strike. I cannot recall very well, but I think those were the main issues. Also, I think there was one on the Muslim side, because there was one soldier, one Dutch soldier, who had been shot and later on died on the way to hospital, and that issue, I think, was also discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You just referred to the BSA conveying a message that they would like the Muslims to leave the enclave. Do you recall whether you had received this ultimatum or heard this ultimatum yourself prior to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had heard that. I had personally heard that, that message earlier, through, I think, Petar or Major Nikolic, one of them or both. But at least I got that information from them, in that there was some orders. I don't know whether we can call them orders or requests, requesting, of course by the BSA, that the Muslims leave the enclave immediately so that they can be safe or they'll be forced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this reference to the Muslims referring to the civilians and military together, or one or the other, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this reference to Muslims actually meant all the people, all the Muslims. You're talking about, whether armed or not, civilians, all of them together. What they meant is they really do not want them there and that they should leave immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to a discussion of air strikes. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we had given the UN HQ the situation of the enclave, and also the various positions of the guns, we also requested for -- for air strikes. These also came earlier from the Muslims, who requested, "Why is the UN not doing anything about this situation?" So we requested for air strikes, and so we were being told that the air strikes would definitely come. There will be air strikes in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the air strikes didn't come right away; is that fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, surprisingly, and to the frustration of us, as the observers, and also Dutch-Bat, no air strikes occurred that morning, so we were afraid that maybe they failed to take place or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do, if anything, that morning when you observed that the air strikes were not happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, you know, when you expect air strikes, you also expect the other side to maybe retaliate because also the air strikes would be there. So we expected them maybe to do something. So, in fact, most of our time there in the morning, we were either in the bunker or somewhere close-by, so that in case of anything, we can go in. But I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were outside the bunker, sir, what, if anything, did you observe outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, outside the compound, what I can remember seeing is some refugees coming in. They started streaming in from Srebrenica. They started coming in. There was an inflow now of refugees to that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I don't think it's in dispute that the close air support was, in fact, delivered that afternoon. Do you recall whether the close air support continued?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the close air support, if we can call it that - because it really wasn't; it was just an air strike - it came in, but came in late, later in the afternoon, and it was not effective. As I can say, it was not effective. By being effective, I mean we had reported to them various positions of guns, of the rocket-launcher, and other military hardware, but surprisingly I think they just managed to hit one tank and one gun or something like that. Having used their six -- six aircraft for that, that was, as far as we were concerned, not effective, because it really did not stop the onslaught on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to providing various positions of guns. Who actually obtained that information and transmitted it, and what was the information? What are you talking about, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, for us, partly as military observers, you know, we had to -- we knew or we could be able to get information on where these positions are. Because when they fire, in fact immediately when you fire, you disclose your position. So it's very easy to know that location. We could go to the map and get the grid references and send it over. But also there were some British guys there. They were -- I think they were calling them JCUs or something, joint combat something, I can't remember, but JCUs, very tough officers, very tough, in that they could penetrate anywhere. They could go anywhere without fear, and they had everything. What I'm saying by "everything" is that they had their weapons. They had the -- they were using a Land Rover, but they had all communication equipment. They could set it up within a very short time, and they were very, very accurate. And in all air strikes, they were the ones directing the aircrafts to the targets, all air strikes -- most of the air strikes anywhere. These were the guys directing the air strikes to the actual target.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, as to any particular reason why the close air support actually stopped that day on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are -- we are not aware -- I was not aware. I was not aware why they stopped, and it is difficult to say the reasons, because at least we expect them to continue until they hit all their targets. But maybe, on the other hand, if you look at it from the other side, maybe they thought they might end up hitting the refugees. But definitely they should have continued on the -- with the air strikes. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, after the air strikes, sir, did you observe any shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the shelling was, you know, resumed straightly. There was a lull, more a lull. Maybe they thought these guys -- the air strikes would continue, so they waited for a while. And after that, the shelling started again. The -- you know, what they did was like they were just doing what they had told us earlier, that if the air strikes actually take place, they're going to bombard the whole place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When do you recall that statement or position being taken by the VRS that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened during a meeting that had been called by the -- by the BSA, and they told us that we should tell the UN not to -- not to execute the air strikes; otherwise, if they do, they'll make sure they wipe out the whole -- the whole enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not you were present for that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. I think I was there in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you have any recollection of who was present? You said you think you were there. Do you have any specific recollection of who was present, where this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting occurred in Bratunac, and the people present normally, you know, in all meetings, Major Nikolic would be there, and Colonel Vukovic was there, and I can't remember the other senior officers who were there. But Andre now was -- I think he was also there, I am not very sure, but at least those two, Nikolic and Vukovic, were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 510, please. And if we could move to -- well, let's look at the first page just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is dated the 11th of July, sir, daily sitrep covering the period of one minute after midnight on the 11th to 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at the top of the English, where it says, it's the second paragraph: "Then the BSA had another ultimatum, Dutch-Bat and the NGOs should leave the enclave, turning over their weapons, the population would be given 48 hours' time to leave the enclave as well. They were also free to go." Colonel, is this the ultimatum that you referred to before or is this another ultimatum? You mentioned that there were a couple of ultimatums that were discussed. I'm just trying to find out, with respect to the section I just read, whether your recollection is whether or not this is the ultimatum you testified about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These -- these ultimatums were there throughout, especially about leaving the enclave. Whenever the BSA were meeting with us or whatever they were communicating to us, these ultimatums were almost similar, these people should leave. But this particular one, I think, was -- this was after. I think it was -- at least this is not the one I talked about, but I think it's -- every time they met us, they were giving us these ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at page 4 of the English and the B/C/S. We'll skip a couple of sections to try to save a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at the entry for 1600 hours, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference to the stream of refugees being uncountable. Towards the bottom, it says: "The latest ultimatum given by the BSA is that if the air strikes continue, everything inside the enclave will be bombed, including UNPROFOR and the other UN organisations." Now, I just want to test your memory a little bit, Colonel. Do you recall whether this is the ultimatum that you were referring to, having heard in Bratunac, or was there another ultimatum that's being reflected here, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see -- as you can see written there, this is the latest ultimatum, meaning there were a series of ultimatums given by the BSA. This one now is after the air strikes had taken place. They said, you know, if the air strikes continue - and it's good to know that this time they were getting bolder and bolder, in fact they were telling the UN, "There is nothing you can do," - so, "Either pack up and go with the Muslims, or we wipe you out, all of you." So they were saying it in no uncertain terms that they don't want anybody to be there. If the air strikes continue, they can do whatever they want in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I guess one of the reasons I'm testing your recollection, Colonel, is that you mentioned your recollection is that you heard a similar ultimatum in Bratunac at some point, and you seem to recall that a Djurcic was present and Vukovic. Do you recall whether or not, on the 11th, you were in any position to leave Potocari for Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. On the 11th, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now let's skip down -- skip a few more questions here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go down and focus on the update at 1910 hours, and we're now on page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Under that entry for 1910, sir, at number 3, the report states that: "From 1844 hours until 1900 hours, the BSA fired 22 rockets/shells from Dugo Polje towards Budak and Gradac." In those 16 minutes, sir, during that time do you recall who counted those rockets?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're the ones -- sorry for that. We're the ones who counted these rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what effect, if any, did those rockets have on the civilians who were gathering at the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sound of -- in the fired weapon, and especially when it's rockets, is very scaring, is very scary for everybody, and especially when they are together in one particular area. You know, the feeling that you are there, your sister is there, your brother, your mother, father, grandmother, and all that, all your relatives are in the same place, and that you can be hit and killed at any moment, really sends a chill down your spine. You feel that anything can happen. So the panic was actually so much in them that that you could not hide. It, you can't easily see it. That happened because we were going out there to check what was happening with them and we could see it. It was written all over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to draw your attention to. That. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, are you in a position to give us the information you promised?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I'm not receiving interpretation. I wish I could understand your language better; but in six years, I haven't managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [In English] Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the joint position of the Defence of Mr. Pandurevic, in view of the circumstances and the time when we received the motion, and in view of the fact that the witness, if he should testify, will do so after the recess, then we would like to ask more time until tomorrow for additional consultations. Then, in the course of tomorrow, we would like to give to you our definitive position. So we are asking to have this extra time until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You will have that extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll indicate our various decisions at the end of today's sitting, which means that you leave us some time. So try to conclude your direct today. If not, we'll continue tomorrow, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to be followed by cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, will you need five minutes or ten minutes at the end, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off talking about the panic that you observed as a result of the over-flying rockets. I want to show you another report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 511, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just note that the first update at 1910 is a continuation of the previous document, 510. So I want to focus your attention on the second update at 2135 hours, sir. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It refers to"another 45 shells over-flying the Dutch-Bat compound between 1845 and 2051 hours, causing a lot of panic amongst the refugees, but they are deliberately missing the buildings." What was the basis of your conclusion, from your observations, that the VRS was deliberately missing the buildings?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our main reason was that these -- we were informed, that is, these shells, we were informed that they were coming from somewhere near the Yellow Bridge towards Bratunac, somewhere there, and they were coming from a tank or tanks. I think there were two tanks or so. So and a tank is very easy to get a direct hit, if you want, and especially in such an area where the ground was tank-able; "tank-able," meaning it was a bit level. It was on the road. So they could easily get a direct hit, if they wanted. We felt at that time that maybe they're firing overhead and not at the people deliberately. Maybe the reasons could have been that now the whole international community knows that the people are centered in one area. So it would have been suicide to actually, on their side, to hit directly where these people were; otherwise, they would attract international condemnation. So that was our own way of reasoning, and that's what we came up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to these two tanks. Now, as to the rockets over-flying the compound, were you able personally ever to see the source of that rocket fire; and if so, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could see and we knew where the rocket-launcher was; and, in fact, even finally, when it got out of that place, it came directly towards Potocari. Actually, we could see it from the same place where we always thought it was. So I personally knew where it was. I knew where it was, and we had given the grid references of the same place. So it was evident that where it was was a definite area; maybe not one place, maybe it was moving about a few metres, then back and all that. But it was the same grid square.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you refer to giving the grid references, sir, just to be clear, you're referring to you provided those grid references in connection with supporting the close air support that you had called for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. We had given that grid reference so that it could have been marked as one of their targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So just to be clear, were these 45 shells in addition to the 22 rockets that you observed previously or would these include the 22?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one thing right now I cannot -- I cannot recall, whether it was an additional. If they were together, I can't remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. That brings us to the 12th of July. Do you recall seeing the Serb forces arrive at the Dutch compound that morning; and if so, can you describe how they appeared and where they went?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this day, okay, started like any other day. But when we woke up, I personally saw that there was some presence of BSA soldiers passing by, passing on the road leading from Bratunac, through Potocari, towards Srebrenica. These soldiers were slightly different from the normal BSA soldiers that we knew, in that they wore -- they wore black. So they passed Potocari; some went straight towards Srebrenica; others branched, I think, to the right somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you see any other soldiers or military forces arrive in Potocari; and if so, what did they do, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, immediately, these soldiers in black passed through Potocari. They were followed almost immediately by now the normal BSA soldiers that we knew, with their camouflage. Those ones now came in and took positions in Potocari, that is, along the road. They started even going towards where the IDPs were. They -- they took their positions, and you could see they were scattered everywhere. They were almost -- they had manned the whole -- the whole area. We then -- there were some who had, I think, blue -- I think they all wore blue. Like the blue uniform was for the police, so we saw these ones now follow immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just for the record, you refer to "IDPs." What is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: IDPs, we're talking about internally-displaced people; in fact, that is what we were referring them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What happened next after these soldiers came in and took up positions along the road and among the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this caused a lot of concern for us because we were thinking that maybe they can do whatever they want. Now that they're already inside, maybe the mop-up exercise could start any time, because immediately when infantry gets in, what they do is to wipe up, to mop up the place, that is, clean the place, clear the place of any element of the enemy. So we thought maybe they're going to attempt to do that. So we forced ourselves, you know, because -- I say the word "force ourselves," because we were fearing them in the process because we don't know what intentions they have. But at the same time, we cannot sit back and watch them doing whatever they want. So we went out to investigate, to check what really was happening, and we found that they were -- they were mingling with the locals, not discussing. But they were there with them, and they were everywhere, everywhere. And most of them could not speak English, so we could not communicate with them properly. You try to talk to someone, and he does not understand what you're talking about, and you also cannot get what -- what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on that note, do you recall where Emir and Hasan were by this time on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this time, Hasan had not reported. He had not come back yet. And, Emir, I can't remember whether he had come back or not. I'm not very sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember investigating any reports of threatening behaviour by the Serb forces towards the refugees early that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was part of the intentions that we had on going out of the Dutch-Bat compound, because we had received information that the BSA soldiers were threatening the Muslims. They were behaving in a manner like they could shoot them. They could shoot them any time. So we went out there to check what was happening, and somehow we didn't find them posing in such a threatening way. In fact, we didn't see them pointing their guns; though, we had been told that they had at the Muslims. That obviously does not mean that they had not pointed at them. But what we were told and what we saw straightly differed. So we didn't see them pointing the guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, in fact, when you went to investigate this report of a threat, what did you actually see the Serb soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, I saw them giving out candies in a friendly way, giving out sweets, bonbon, or whatever they were calling it. So they were giving it to them, and, you know, it looked like they are doing it without any -- without any problems. Like it was out of their own hearts that they were giving out. But, later on, we noticed that immediately we turned. You know, we moved from that place, and they were taking them back. So it was like an act, they were acting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall there being more than one occasion when you saw candy or sweets being distributed by the Serb soldiers to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the first time; but, later on, I witnessed one, when General Ratko Mladic came in, and, okay, a lot of activities happened. But the moment I told him that there were some men who were put in one place, they were isolated. They were in a place where the -- the place was not habitable. At that time, he went there and distributed some beers and all that. Also before we went there, in the field where I found him, he was distributing those candies with the soldiers there. And, immediately after, now he turned to another direction to find the candies being taken by the same soldiers, and you wonder why this is happening. But that was happening in front of cameras. That is when they were giving the candies. It was happening in front of the cameras, and my assumption was that maybe they're just acting maybe to show that they are friendly to these people. They don't mean any harm to them. But the reason why they should take back the candies, really, you can't understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to encountering General Mladic, and you stated that some things happened. Would you tell the Trial Chamber about your encounters and any discussions you had with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the first place, I just bumped into him when I -- when I was getting out of the Dutch-Bat compound. I saw a lot of soldiers grouped together somewhere, and I wondered what was going on. So I went there out of curiosity to check what is happening. And from a distance, I could see one similar guy, you know. He is a bit short, and there was some distance between him and the other people. So you could tell he was the main guy there, the main character. So I approached and I looked at the guy, and I saw he's General Mladic. At least I could identify him, because he's someone we had seen on TV and all that. So you could easily identify him. So I knew this is the actual, the real General Ratko Mladic. So I approached him through a series of those soldiers that were there, the bodyguards and the senior officers. And, finally, I managed to get where he was. And upon seeing me, he looked at me and saw my patch, that is, it's Kenyan, and he asked me, "Oh, are you Kenyan," and I told him, "Yes, I am Kenyan." Then we started talking and discussing issues. He talked about athletics in Kenya. We talked about another general who was in another sector that he was operating. We discussed a lot of issues, a lot of outside issues, issues which are not to do with the real situation in that -- in the enclave. So we discussed freely and we finished. I left him a bit, then later on returned after I realised that there was something queer happening, that there was separation of men and women and children, and that the men were being taken to -- to one particular building. They were being taken to a building somewhere there. Then I looked across and saw the building and the people that were being taken there. I came back to the general and I asked him, "Surely, what is happening here? I can see men are being separated from women and children and being taken to that building. The way it looks from the outside really shows that there is a big problem. It's overcrowded. How can you keep people in one overcrowded place like that? There's no air, there's no space, there's nothing." So I asked him those questions and we talked. Then he looked at me and asked me whether -- I mean, he told me that, yeah, as far as he's concerned, the people there are very comfortable. He told me that he'll take me there, himself, because for information I tried to go there earlier and I was stopped by the BSA soldiers. I was told I could not go there. So this time the general told me, "I'll take you there myself." So at that time we started talking; and within a very short time, he said, "Let's go." We went there, and actually we saw the people were there huddled in one particular building, and you could see there's no space in between. It was overcrowded, and they were making noises, you know, shouting - not shouting, as such - but you could see they were murmuring to show that they were dissatisfied and all that. So I told him, "This is not acceptable. This is wrong," and he told me, "No, no, no. It's not, it's not. Look at them, they're okay." At that time, a soldier started distributing beer. The beer soldier started distributing beer, candies, and all that, sodas, soft drinks. You know, he started distributing; and at that time, the fuming was going on. This was meant now to show that the people were comfortable, which was not the actual case, because the situation had not changed. So I told him, "Okay. If they are comfortable, fine, but what do you intend to do? What is the problem here? Why are you separating them?" He told me, "No, no, no. They're okay. Just leave them alone." So I finished with the general at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you try to get access to those men in that building when you were brought back there by General-- or with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I requested that I go in to check, physically, but he told me point blank, "You cannot go in there." He refused me entry into that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what happened next, to your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing to note here is that when these men were being taken inside that building, they were being forced to abandon their wear wares, their belongings, on the way somewhere. They were told to drop them there and go in, everything that they had. We're talking about maybe even wallets, their bundle of clothes, or whatever they were carrying, to leave them there, and they're going into the building. So later on, after I was denied permission to get in there, I -- I just went back. I just went back. I can't remember anything else around there, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified a few moments ago that you noticed that the men were being separated. Can you describe, in as much detail as you can, what you actually observed of those separations, how the men were reacting, and what, if anything, you tried to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this separation was actually very bad. I did not enjoy it. I did not like it, in that you could see men were being moved from their families. They were being told, "All the men, come over here." Now, initially, they had indicated that the ones they were looking for, even when Major Nikolic had gone inside the Dutch-Bat compound, had indicated the people they were looking for were those who were in the fighting age. So after they started picking these men and taking them to that building, there was a lot of fear from amongst themselves and also the families they're leaving behind, in that no one could know for sure what their fate would be. So as they got out, they could be given most of the things that the family had. You could see that happening, "Oh, please go with that, go with that." Sometimes they, themselves, could leave whatever they had with the families that they were leaving behind. So it was total confusion, because they didn't know who was safe. Is it the families? Is it the men who were being moved? So who was safe, no one could tell. So sometimes in that confusion, everyone was shedding tears, crying here and there, the families, the soldiers themselves -- the men themselves. And with that confusion, we could see that definitely this is a state that we should not have reached in the first place. So they were separated, kept together, huddled together in that one group. And after that, the aim - I talked to some of the BSA soldiers - was exactly to make sure that they can be able to identify those who are soldiers in the war, and so that they can take them elsewhere. So I think that that maybe will come later; but as for now, that is what I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was doing the separating, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this separation was being done by the BSA soldiers who were there, but their senior leaders were also there, because even General Mladic was there. These other Colonels, they were all there, Major Nikolic, Colonel Vukovic, and all those senior officers, they were all there. They were all there when this separation was going on. The actual removal of the people was being done by the soldiers, but they were obviously the ones who were giving the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You recall buses arriving at some point on the 12th, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that very well, because I was directly involved in a discussion with General Mladic, telling him that a situation has arrived whereby the UN is going to send buses to come and pick the refugees from there. And upon telling him that, he told me, point blank, he does not require the use or the help from the UN. He, himself, has organised his own transport, and he's going to transport those people from there to Tuzla, where their Muslim brothers are located. Those were his words, "We will move the Muslims from here and take them to Tuzla to join their brothers there." So, immediately, somehow it was like in a movie. Almost immediately after, about 20, 30 minutes or so, the buses started arriving, and we saw them come in. They aligned themselves now facing the other direction now towards Bratunac. After they turned, they faced Bratunac. Now in their own lane, they came in, ready to exit after taking the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of follow-up questions, sir. During all these conversations that you described between yourself and General Mladic and various Serb soldiers, who was doing the interpreting or how were you actually communicating?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was very difficult at that time because for sure they could not allow our interpreters to come anywhere near there, and also we did not want to come with them there. So what we were doing, we were trying to identify some of the BSA soldiers who could understand and speak English, and somehow, myself, I managed to get one. Of course, the legal officer I had alluded to earlier was speaking good English; but as a senior officer, he could not be available throughout. So I selected one -- this one guy who could speak a bit of English. He was a bit conspicuous, I think, in that I think he was wearing a blue -- a blue UN jacket. So at least that one could speak a bit of -- a bit of English. He's the one now I was telling so that he could tell these other people. So he was the link. And wherever he moved, you know, I would try and make sure that if there's anything I want to communicate to the BSA, he's there to help us. Otherwise, communication was a big, big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you observe anyone boarding the buses that had arrived, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the boarding of the buses was, you know, commenced immediately thereafter, and we were there to see them, to witness that they are going in, and that they are going in there properly. And during this period, the -- there was something that the BSA were doing. They were seeing -- you know, when the women and children were now going to the buses, they could look at them. And if they identify a boy who is slightly above 14, 15, 16, somewhere there, they could turn to him, they could chuck him out, and tell him to go to the building where the men were grouped. That was to my amazement, because they had said they don't want the young and the very old. So I asked some of the soldiers, "Why are you picking these very young boys," and due to their problem with their communication, you know, they could not understand. But they were still telling them to go in, so later on I started removing some of the boys. I could ask them their ages, personally I could ask them their ages. I would say, "What is your age," and the boy would say, "Fourteen." I would tell them, "Get out. Fourteen, get out." After they got out, I could show them their way back through these BSA soldiers, and I would tell them, "No, no. These are just boys. Leave them alone." Now, on the way out, after I got out of these, when I turned back, I could still some more being still told to go in. So it was like a vicious circle, but I know at least I managed to save several of them. Several, actually, did not get into those buses, but I could not be there throughout. So some of them, I'm sure still were forced into those buses, and they were young.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe the actual process that you observed of the -- let's start with the people other than the men in the house. Did you see them getting on the buses? Can you describe what that process was like?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the process was not that honourable, in that they were not being requested to get in. In fact, they were being pushed in. And in the moment you tried to either resist or maybe try to shout at your brother or sister, your relatives, that they come to the same bus, you could be pushed even to the ground by force.
