Because, you know, I wish you could be able to look at yourself in such a situation, in that you're seeing yourself being forced into a bus and your sister or your brother or any close relative is now entering a different bus, and you want them to join you where you are or you want to go back and join them where they are. The people you're telling that. They are telling you, "No, no, no. Go in. Go in, go in. Go in." The moment you try that, you are forced. You are pushed to the ground. You are pushed until you physically get in. They start crying. They start making a lot of noises, "Why are you doing this do us?" "What is wrong?" "What have we done?" You know, a lot of issues were coming up, and it was to do with, "Why should you people be doing this to us?" We were ourselves now we also hear some of the -- I mean, we could understand some or part of the language because we were there for some time, but not fully. But we could hear the outcry of the Muslims being pushed to go into those buses, and it was not the most comfortable position or situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, have an occasion to observe any of the men from this house getting on buses or leaving on buses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH  KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did. When the men were being taken to the buses, for one, they were not allowed to go back and pick their belongings. So they were being put in the buses without their belongings, without the items that they were forced to leave out there. So they were taken towards the buses one by one, like they are prisoners of war, one by one, one following each other, with no space in between, and soldiers everywhere. And in between the buses, there are soldiers to ensure that one does not cross. So they were all taken in, and this was one of the saddest moments that I ever had in that area, in that you could see men, real men, crying, asking us, "You, UNPROFOR, why are you letting these people take us? Why are you letting them go with us? Why do you want us to be killed by these people?" And we could ask them, you know, "What do you think they're going to do to you," and they say, "Really, these people are going to kill to us. Why do they, in the first place, separate us from our families? Why are they taking us in buses? Do you know where these buses are going to?" And it's true, we really did not know, other than what we had been told, that they would take the Muslims to Tuzla. So there was -- it was very emotional, in that some of the men, obviously, we were seeing them in the village of Srebrenica, so some of them we could identify, this is so-and-so, this one looks familiar and all that, and all these people are crying, looking at you for assistance, assistance you cannot provide. They're also desperate. There's nothing you can do, and you know for sure these guys are headed to a place where maybe it's not very safe, but there's nothing you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we still have a couple of minutes before the five minutes. My next idea was to go to a document, though, that may take a little bit longer. I'd ask if we could continue tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kingori, we need you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you'll be escorted, and thank you so much. Tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there is this Josse motion that he referred to earlier on, which we have gone through during the break. Will you be in a position to respond to it orally tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the Gvero motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other Defence teams, insofar as considering some of the points made by the Gvero Defence team in their motion, they may be of relevance to some of you? I beg your pardon, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I haven't read it yet, Your Honour. We were in court, so I didn't get a copy yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But, anyway, it's an appointment for tomorrow. We will be discussing this orally; and then, if necessary, we'll either hand an oral decision tomorrow or else a written one in the course of the recess. We'll also discuss tomorrow, after hearing your position, if there is anything to be said in relation to the Prosecution motion to add another witness. So we could do that. Who had the intention of going first cross-examining this witness from amongst you? You, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still require two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At least two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least two hours. I think there will be two hours left. We'll see tomorrow, anyway, we'll see tomorrow. In the meantime, I would suggest that you start preparing. The worst that could happen is that you'll go home and be more ready when you return in January, more ready when you return in January, to start your cross-examination. Anyway, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, we have had an opportunity to discuss, during the break, the joint Defence oral application for an extension of the time limit set in our scheduling order for the filing of the 65 ter documents. We have taken into consideration not only what we consider to be a justified request, but also the fact that the Prosecution does not object to that, rather it's signified its agreement with such need to have the time limit extended, so we have decided to grant it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the 65 ter documents that the written scheduling order refers to, the time limit will be as requested, end of April instead of end of March, with two important caveats. Most important, of course, is that nothing else is going to change. The other dates fixed for the pre-Defence case conference and start of Defence case will stand. The other caveat is that we believe that the point made by the Prosecution, in relation to expert reports, shouldn't fall within the extension -- extended time limit, but that those reports should be handed to the Prosecution, be made available to the Prosecution, by the 31st of March, as originally planned. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think our agreement was limited to just the military expert, so that there's no confusion. We would just like that clarification from Your Honours. We agreed that we were going to tender to them only the military expert by the 31st of March, and all the other experts, if any, we would tender to them by the 30th of April, pursuant to the extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- thank you, Mr. Ostojic. That's how you understood it to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, then that's how it will be. I think it's clear enough. Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify just one other point a little more. The Court, Your Honour, refers to 65 ter documents. Just so there's no confusion, it was the 65 ter witness list and the documents. So I just want to make sure we're all on the same page. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, whatever the 31st March deadline that we had indicated in our scheduling order refers to, okay, are the filings that we had in mind and which we still have in mind. The other thing is this: We are granting this extension with the understanding that within the same time frame, that is, the end of April, 30th of April, you will come forward with a definitive -- both of you, a definitive position in relation to agreed facts and possibly adjudicated facts. In other words, in the interim between our Rule 98 bis decision and the 65 ter filings, you need to engage yourselves into an exchange of correspondence on possible agreed facts and possible adjudicated facts, and have that crystallised by the time the 65 ter filings take place. All right? I think we can adjourn now. Tomorrow, 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
